consensus_summary: Consensus primary meaning is the eye as lamp of the body signifying spiritual perception, moral condition, and inner light/darkness (Matt 6:22-23 etc.), with common alternatives of divine omniscience/watchfulness (eyes of the Lord), the good/evil eye as generosity vs. stinginess/envy, and lust/desire.
book_summary: The lamp of the body—a burning light within a person, shining as the stars shine; the good eye gives its bread to the poor, the evil eye withholds; His eyes are flames of fire, running to and fro through all the earth.
consensus_core_identification: Eye as lamp of the body for spiritual/moral perception and condition (primary), plus divine eyes for omniscience and good/evil eye for generosity/stinginess (common alts).
book_core_identification: Lamp of the body as inner burning light shining like stars; good/evil eye as giving vs. withholding bread; divine eyes as flames of fire ranging the earth.
boundary_disagreement: Book unifies lamp-of-body with the generosity/stinginess idiom as co-present readings of the same symbol and adds a star-shining celestial precision (cross-referenced to another chapter) not present in consensus treatments of the lamp verses; consensus often separates the spiritual-perception reading from the Semitic-generosity idiom as alternatives and does not link the eye-lamp to stars.
rationale: Minimum cores match exactly on the three main strands (lamp/spiritual light, good/evil eye as giving/withholding, divine eyes ranging the earth) that dominate the consensus primary and common alternatives; the book simply compresses them into one entry using the same verses. Differences are precision (burning/star-like light) and presentation (unified rather than ranked primary-vs-alt), which refine boundaries without replacing the referents or contradicting any consensus claim. Extra detail such as star-shining is therefore not allowed to force divergence.
strongest_objection: The distinctive addition of 'shining as the stars shine' and the seamless fusion of the lamp metaphor with the generosity idiom may reflect the book's private symbolic system rather than mainstream consensus boundaries for those verses.
